extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary/theological criticism; scholars interested in rhetoric, religious writing, and the reformers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative points for producing or judging religious/literary commentary and criticism, especially on theological subjects (e.g., Luther, Newman) with attention to rhetoric, accessibility, and intellectual balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commentary should be practical, popular, and highly rhetorical
rubrics_metrics.description: "commentary is practical, popular, and highly rhetorical ... not scientific"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page privileges commentary that addresses ordinary readers (practical, popular) and uses rhetorical force rather than purely scientific or academic exposition; nevertheless the author expects the rhetoric to be defensible ("though I think that every word of it[n] scientifically defended"). Anti-pattern: treating popular/rhetorical style as a license for indefensible claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify access to the reader (simplify the access of the soul to God)
rubrics_metrics.description: "his determination, powerfully carried out, to simplify the access of the soul to God"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor clear, direct pathways in exposition — 'a straight and short passage' — that make difficult religious truths readily available to readers. Example: Luther's efforts to remove clerical gatekeeping so ordinary hearers can approach the Word. Anti-pattern: overcomplicating doctrines with needless institutional or ceremonial obstacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address and be intelligible to 'simple hearers' and popular audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: The author notes that the simple hearers expected truth set forth plainly and found Luther useful: 'the simple hearers, who expect that the t[eacher] will set forth what is true rather than what is false... these found him [Luther] instructive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt tone, examples, and emphasis to non-specialist readers; avoid modes of exposition that presuppose specialist background. Anti-pattern: producing work intelligible only to 'systematic divines' or specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rhetorical extravagance that obscures meaning ('tiger-lilies' of speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: "the 'heroic man's' rhetorical atroc[ities], 'tiger-lilies' of speech ... capable of an innocent meaning at least; they are but wolves' clothing"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical flourishes can be effective but risk misinterpretation or being used by opponents as a charge of extravagance; use ornamentation responsibly and be aware how ornament may be weaponized in controversy. Anti-pattern: letting 'spent rockets' (overblown metaphors) be taken by adversaries as decisive refutation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be direct and decisive in argumentation; avoid mere feints
rubrics_metrics.description: "keeps gazing at him with a look of deep horror, but rather makes feints than really strikes him" (critique of ineffectual argumentation)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong critical writing should aim clear, substantial claims and direct refutations rather than evasive or purely ornamental attacks. Anti-pattern: producing clever-looking but substantively ineffectual criticisms (feints) that fail to engage the main point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance analysis with imaginative synthesis (collect the many into the one)
rubrics_metrics.description: "They are analysers... want that imaginative power, — so necessary in religion, — which brings the many into one"; also: "collect the possibility, but forget the inference."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical or philosophical writing should not only dissect (analysis) but also synthesize — draw unifying inferences and imaginative wholes that make meaning for readers. Anti-pattern: shattering arguments into pieces without reconstructive vision, leaving readers with possibilities but no guiding inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve moral and spiritual feeling while employing critical thought
rubrics_metrics.description: "the critical philosophy cultivates the moral sense while it [does not blunt] the eye of reason... It is of the highest poetry... cognate with religion" contrasted with "the mechanical philosophy blunts the religious susceptibilities"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use critical methods that deepen moral/spiritual understanding rather than suppress emotional or religious sensibility; prefer modes of critique that harmonize with poetic/spiritual insight rather than mechanistic reduction. Anti-pattern: adopting purely mechanical critique that perverts or deadens religious feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate practical abuses with doctrinal theories
rubrics_metrics.description: "let them be hunted out and not confounded with theories and confessions of faith" — practical falsehoods and heresies should be separated from formal theological theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating institutions or practices, distinguish between corrupt/practical abuses (e.g., superstitious practices, mummeries) and the underlying doctrinal positions; do not let practical corruption stand as a refutation of the doctrine itself. Scoring note: treat examples of malpractice as distinct from the intellectual merits of a theological system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer authenticity, fervor, and tenderness of spirit in religious writing
rubrics_metrics.description: "he loved his fervor and reality of religious feeling, tenderness of his spirit, the vehement eloquence with which he assails..." (praise for Luther's tone and spirit)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value writing that exhibits genuine religious feeling and moral earnestness; passionate sincerity and moral earnestness can be strengths (even when stylistically rough). Anti-pattern: dismissing authors solely for rhetorical roughness while ignoring their authentic moral force.
